name: Designing Aircraft
description: How airships, balloons and planes are laid out to fly well.

pages.title: Designing Aircraft
pages.text:
[#](FFFFFF)[#]() **Key points**

- Every block is weight to lift and drag to push.
- Envelope: round, **2 to 3 times as long as wide**, tapering to the tail.
- **Engines inside**, where the crew refuels them; shafts carry the power out.
- Push **through the middle of the drag**.

Lift, weight, push and drag decide how an aircraft flies. Hot air lifts by the cubic metre it fills, the air drags on every envelope block and on the ship's weight, and propellers push only up to their airflow. Good designs come from those four, not from a look.

pages.title: The envelope
pages.text: Each envelope block drags about as much as three blocks' worth of the ship's weight, whatever the envelope's shape, and each m3 of hot air holds up about 1.5 mass low down, less higher up. So a fatter envelope carries more for its skin: an 11-wide one holds about 0.75 m3 per block, a 13-wide one about 0.9.

pages.title: Its shape
pages.text: About 2 to 3 times as long as it is wide reads as an airship, points into the wind and stays cheap to push. Round in every cross-section (a stepped circle, never a square), blunt at the nose, fullest about two fifths back, then tapering to a point at the tail. A sphere is a hot air balloon.

pages.title: Sizing it
pages.text: Size the envelope to the load, with room to climb: about 1.2 m3 of hot air per mass of ship takes it to y 200. A bigger envelope only adds drag, a smaller one won't climb. Each Hot Air Burner fills 500 m3.

pages.title: The gondola
pages.text: Hang the gondola under the envelope's belly, touching it or on posts, a little forward of the envelope's middle, since a tail propeller, fins and shafts weigh on the stern. Keep it compact: a cabin with the helm at the bow and the engine room behind.

pages.title: Hanging level
pages.text: A balloon hangs with its weight straight under the centre of its air. A compact airship's air centres only 2 to 4 blocks above its weight, so one block of gondola along the keel tips it 5 to 10 degrees. The tapering tail is more skin than air, so a bare envelope hangs tail-down.

pages.title: Engines and fuel
pages.text: Put every engine where the crew walks: an engine room in the gondola, reached along its floor from the helm and warm inside it. A ship whose engines sit on platforms outside drifts helpless once their fuel runs out, because nobody can reach them in flight.

pages.title: Shafts through the skin
pages.text: Carry the power from the engine room to the propellers by shafts: up through the belly and along inside the envelope. Where a shaft passes through the skin, an envelope-encased shaft keeps the balloon sealed. Shafts weigh little; a platform for an engine is dead weight.

pages.title: Weight
pages.text: Dead weight costs twice: once to lift, with more envelope that drags, and once to push. Each block of weight costs about four times its own drag in the envelope that holds it up. Leave out decks and platforms nothing stands on, solid walls where trapdoors or panes will do, and iron blocks for balance.

pages.title: Where it pushes
pages.text: Nearly all the drag is the envelope, so push in line with its middle. Propellers low under it tip the nose up at speed, high ones tip it down. Good places: one big propeller on the envelope's axis ahead of the nose, where its weight evens out the tail's, or behind the tail; or a pair at its widest point on short shaft arms through its sides.

pages.title: Level at full speed
pages.text: The gondola drags too, so the drag's middle sits a shade under a round envelope's axis: a push a tenth of a block above it dips the nose a degree or two at full speed. Each block of envelope ridge on top lifts that middle a little, a row more height (shaft on the round axis) half a block; a lower open deck lowers it.

pages.title: Big slow fans
pages.text: A Propeller Bearing pushes 0.2 x sails^1.5 x RPM for 2 stress units per sail per RPM, so the same engines push harder on a bigger fan. Each Portable Engine gives 2048 stress units: four of them turn 28 sails at 128 RPM, pushing about 3800.

pages.title: Fins
pages.text: Fins of Symmetric Sails at the tail (a cross, or three in a Y) keep it pointing ahead, and set along the line of flight they cost little going straight. A fin alone on a Swivel Bearing turns a big airship only slowly.

pages.title: Steering
pages.text: One Steering Wheel at the helm, its shafts running to a Swivel Bearing under the tail with a Wooden Propeller on it, powered through the bearing from the drive line: turned, it swings the stern round. A ship with a pair of propellers can steer by slowing one side instead.

pages.title: Hot air balloons
pages.text: A hot air balloon is the simple early aircraft: a round envelope as wide as it is tall, a basket hung under it on posts from its corners, a burner. It climbs, sinks and drifts with the wind. Propellers on the basket push low and tip it at speed: keep them small and slow.

pages.title: Planes
pages.text: A plane flies only while it moves, so it must be light: a slim body, long fabric wings over the weight's centre, a tail far back with a flat stabiliser and an upright fin, engines behind the pilot and propellers out on the wings so the pilot sees ahead, Grindstones for landing gear. No plane holds itself level here: it needs a Gyroscope. See [#](2E5AAC)[Propellers](entry://flight/propellers)[#]().

pages.title: Built solid
pages.text:
Every part should meet the blocks beside it where their shapes touch; glue holds a part that doesn't, but it hangs in the air with a gap round it. A sail is a thin panel across the middle of its block, so it joins blocks beside it, not one above or below; a Grindstone under a top slab hangs half a block clear.\
\
Close a body's sides with stairs, walls, trapdoors or panes so no sky shows through it, and case its gearing (encased cogwheels, casings) instead of leaving bare cogs sticking out.

pages.title: Choosing the wings
pages.text:
Lift grows with speed, and every block is weight, so the wing block sets a plane's size. A two-seater on sails needs two wings about 27 blocks across. Copycat Wings (8m) lift half again as much for the same weight: two of them about 21 across, or a single wing about 27 across, which sails can't carry.\
\
Wider wings climb higher; round tips look softer but lift a little less.

pages.title: A blimp that hauls
pages.text: [#](FFFFFF)[#]() **In depth.** An 11 by 11 by 25 envelope (about 600 m3) over a closed 7 by 10 gondola with the helm, barrels, a smoker, a crafting table and two Hot Air Burners. Four Portable Engines in its engine room turn a 28-sail Propeller Bearing behind the tail at 128 RPM.

It cruises at about 9 blocks a second, climbs past y 250 and turns about 4 degrees a second. The drive shaft runs up through the belly and along the envelope's axis to the fan; a branch drives a Wooden Propeller on a Swivel Bearing under the tail, which the Steering Wheel swings.

pages.title: Ask the Book
pages.text: Where the book has its voice, ask it for an airship and it lays one out to your wishes (open deck or cabin, beds, chests, speed, height), balanced to hang level, as a 3D model you can save as a schematic. Ask it for a small plane (one or two seats) and it designs one that flies from a short field, with one wing or two, sails or Copycat Wings, round or square tips, to suit what you want and can make. Ask it for a helicopter (one to three seats) and it lays one out on a gyroscopic rotor, balanced and checked.
